newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - It's auction time.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - It's auction time.

text.p: Attention in the U.S. Treasury market shifts to supply on Tuesday, day one of the three-part quarterly refunding.

The Treasury kicks off its $38 billion auction party with the sale of $16 billion in three-year notes on Tuesday afternoon. On Wednesday, $12 billion in 10-year notes are up for sale, followed by the auction of $10 billion in 30-year bonds on Thursday.
Little price action is expected until after the auctions are over.
Late Monday, the when-issued three-year note was at 6.017 percent. As recently as last Thursday, the three-year was yielding as low as 5.85 percent.

"With three-years on the cheap side of 6 percent, you will have buyers," said a head trader at a primary dealership. But a decline below 6 percent may force accounts to wait, let dealers buy them and buy from the dealers later, he said.
"I think the Street will be smart about it," the trader said, predicting a rate of 6.03-6.04 percent.

Yields soared on Friday, as prices tumbled on the heels of stronger-than-expected data on the labor market, which included a decline in the unemployment rate to 4.8 percent in July from 5.0 percent in June. There was also a second report of a strengtening manufacturing sector.
Treasuries, which plunged more than two points on Friday, fell again on Monday, with the 30-year bond down 12/32 to 101-29/32 to yield 6.48 percent.

"Even though the market sold off on Friday there are many positives for ther market that are still at work," said Pat Alexander, head trader at BancAmerica Securities, citing the favorable supply picture.
Not much activity was forecast ahead of the auction, although some said position squaring could push yields a bit higher.

Alexander noted that Friday's selloff has changed the attitude of the market somewhat, in that "people are now returning to value investing." He said that last week, "people were buying price action as opposed to prices."

Also of interest on Tuesday, but unlikely to garner much response, are the BTM-Schroders weekly chain store index at 0900 EDT/1300 GMT, the Conference Board's leading indicators index for June at 1000 EDT and the Redbook weekly retail sales report at 1455 EDT.
Meanwhile, Federal Reserve of San Francisco president Robert Parry is slated to speak on the economy in Salt Lake City at 1500 EDT.
